fur: Before any colour goes down, impress whiskers and a few stray pale hairs into the paper with an empty ballpoint pen, so they stay light when you shade over them.
Build the main colour in short, tapering flicks that follow the way the fur grows, leaving slivers of bare paper between them.
Add the darkest colour last, only where the fur parts or tucks into shadow, and keep those strokes as short as the rest.
feather: Sketch where the larger feathers overlap with the lightest possible pressure, like roof tiles running from head to tail.
Layer the colour in strokes that follow each feather's shaft, and darken a thin band just under every overlapping edge so the feathers sit on top of one another.
Burnish only the glossy wing and tail feathers, and leave the fluffy breast grainy and unburnished.
skin: Put the spots, warts or markings in first with a sharp point, then colour around and over them in thin layers.
Shade in small overlapping circles rather than straight strokes, blending each colour into the next so the surface looks smooth instead of streaky.
For wet or glossy skin, keep a few crisp specks of bare paper for the shine and burnish right up to their edges.
shell: Let every stroke follow the curve of the shell, so the marks themselves describe the dome or the spiral.
Lay the speckles, bands or ridges over a pale base, pressing harder on the side turned away from the light.
For a polished shell, keep a bright patch of paper for the highlight and burnish the rest; for an eggshell, stop before the wax turns shiny.
wing: Draw the veins or the outline of the pattern first with a needle-sharp point and the lightest pressure you can manage.
Fill each cell between the veins with smooth, even layers, building the colour slowly rather than pressing hard.
For see-through wings, colour the background through them a shade paler, then add a faint cool layer and keep the edges crisp.
petal: Shade each petal from its base outwards, pressing more firmly near the centre and easing off towards the edge.
Let your strokes follow the faint veins and ripples, and keep the layers thin so the paper glows through the colour.
Where one petal tucks behind another, darken the back one with a cooler shade of the same colour rather than grey, and let the colour temperature do the work.
foliage: Cover the whole leaf with a pale yellow or light green first, since it brightens every green you layer on top.
Work the darker greens in from the edges and around the veins, leaving the veins as negative space in the lighter layer underneath.
For deep shade among the leaves, mix a chromatic dark from your darkest green and a red or purple instead of using Black.
bark: Lay a mid-brown with the side of the lead, letting the grain of the paper break it up into a rough texture for free.
Draw the cracks and ridges with a sharp, dark pencil, running them the way the bark grows and using hatching to deepen the grooves.
Catch the light along the raised edges with bare paper or a pale colour, and dab on lichen with a yellow-green.
stone: Block in the base colour in loose circles with the side of the lead, so the grain of the paper shows through as grit.
Speckle and vein the stone with a sharp point, varying the pressure so some marks fade away and others stay crisp.
Shade the underside with a cool colour and add a dark cast shadow where it meets the ground, so the stone looks properly heavy.
ceramic: Decide where the shine sits before you start, and keep that shape as bare paper all the way through.
Build the glaze in thin layers that wrap around the form, then burnish for a hard finish and wipe off any wax bloom with a tissue.
Let a hint of the table colour creep into the shadow side, since glazed pots reflect whatever is beside them.
glass: Draw what you can see through the glass rather than the glass itself, a shade paler and slightly bent out of shape.
Put the darkest accents along the rim, the base and the edges, where the glass is thickest.
Leave the brightest streaks as untouched paper, and if one gets covered, try lifting it back with a dab of sticky tape.
metal: Look for the sharp jumps in value: polished metal reflects in hard-edged bands, not gentle gradients.
Lay those bands in with crisp edges, borrowing blues and browns from the surroundings instead of using grey alone.
Burnish the whole surface firmly and save the brightest glints as bare paper, so it gleams.
fabric: Lay the main colour over the whole cloth in a light layer, adding a faint cross-hatching if it's a woven fabric like linen or tweed.
Shade the folds by pressing harder in the creases and easing off over the ridges, where the cloth catches the light.
Add stripes, checks or sprigs last, bending them as they cross a fold so the pattern sits in the cloth.
wool: Map the lumps of fleece or the rows of stitches lightly, as loose curls or small V shapes.
Shade the underside of each curl or stitch and leave the tops paler, so the texture looks raised.
Keep the pressure moderate and the paper grain showing, as burnishing would flatten all the fluff.
wood: Lay a pale, warm base in long strokes along the grain, using the side of the lead.
Draw the grain lines and knots with a sharper, darker pencil, letting them wobble and wander the way real grain does.
For polished wood, burnish with your lightest warm colour; for weathered wood, keep the grainy texture and add a cool grey-blue in the cracks.
paper: Leave most of the paper as paper, since a white or cream object needs only a few pale shadows to read.
Shade creases and folds with a pale cool colour, crisp along one side of the fold and fading out on the other.
Keep the pressure light throughout, because heavy wax turns shiny and paper should look matt.
crust: Start with a pale warm yellow over the whole crust, then build the browns on top, darkest where it baked hardest.
Work the browns in small scumbling circles so the grain of the paper shows through as crumbly texture.
Burnish a glazed top firmly with your lightest warm colour, but leave the cut side and the crumb rough and pale.
fruit: Find the brightest highlight and draw a faint ring round it, so you remember to leave it as bare paper.
Layer the local colour in strokes that curve around the fruit, dropping a touch of green into the shadow of a red one, or purple into a yellow one.
Burnish firmly with White or your lightest colour over everything but the highlight, so the skin looks taut and glossy.
liquid: Colour the surface of a drink or soup in smooth, level strokes, slightly darker towards the far side of the bowl or cup.
Leave a clean sliver of paper where the light reflects, and a darker line where the liquid meets its container.
For a water drop, put the darkest part on the side facing the light, a glow on the far side and a speck of bare paper for the highlight.

glossary.burnish: Press firmly with a light colour or a blender pencil to melt the wax layers into a smooth, shiny finish.
glossary.layer: One light pass of colour. Coloured pencils build up best in several thin layers rather than one heavy one.
glossary.value: How light or dark a colour is. Get the values right and the colours can be almost anything.
glossary.wax bloom: A cloudy, whitish haze that can rise on heavy layers of wax-based pencil. Wipe it away gently with a tissue.
glossary.toned paper: Paper in a colour other than white, such as tan, grey or black. It gives you a ready-made middle tone, so you only add the lights and darks.
glossary.chromatic dark: A dark made by layering deep colours, such as a dark green with a red or purple, instead of using black. It looks richer and livelier.
glossary.colour temperature: Whether a colour leans warm (towards red, orange and yellow) or cool (towards blue, green and violet). Warm colours seem to come forward and cool ones to sit back.
glossary.impress: Press a line into the paper with a blunt point before colouring. The pencil skims over the dent and leaves a fine pale line, perfect for whiskers and veins.
glossary.hatching: Shading with rows of parallel strokes. The closer the lines, the darker it reads.
glossary.cross-hatching: Hatching in two or more directions, one set laid across another, for darker values or a woven look.
glossary.scumbling: Shading in small, overlapping circles or squiggles, for an even, slightly textured surface with no visible strokes.
glossary.lifting: Taking colour back off the paper by dabbing it with sticky tape or a kneadable eraser. It works best on light layers that haven't been burnished.
glossary.blending: Smoothing one colour into another, either by layering them lightly or by burnishing them together.
glossary.local colour: The actual colour of a thing before light and shadow change it. A tomato's local colour is red, even where its shadow side looks nearly purple.
glossary.negative space: The shapes around and between things. Colouring up to an edge, instead of drawing the thing itself, is a neat way to leave pale shapes behind.
glossary.blender pencil: A colourless wax pencil for blending and burnishing without adding colour. White or your lightest colour can stand in for one.

paper.dark: Black or navy paper makes White and Indigo Blue glow. Put White down first under any pale colour so it doesn't sink into the dark.
paper.tan: Kraft or tan paper gives you a free mid-tone. Add only the lights and the darks, and let the paper do the rest.
paper.grey: Grey paper gives you a calm middle value, so press White firmly for the highlights and let a dark do the shadows.
paper.white: White paper is your brightest highlight, so decide where the light sits and leave those spots untouched from the very start.
